planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Whitewater combines a graceful weeping habit with heart-shaped leaves boldly marked in white and cream, giving it striking multi-season interest beyond the typical redbud's spring flower display.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting where its cascading branches have room to arch downward without crowding. Whitewater is a weeping redbud cultivar whose branches cascade gracefully from a central leader, giving it a fountain-like silhouette distinct from the typical vase-shaped redbud form. In early spring, the bare, pendulous branches are covered in the classic rosy-pink pea-like flowers typical of the species, followed by heart-shaped leaves heavily variegated in white and cream over green, a striking combination that provides ornamental interest all summer rather than just during the brief spring bloom. Because variegated foliage photosynthesizes less efficiently than solid green leaves, growth is somewhat slower than standard redbud cultivars, and the tree stays more compact, making it a good choice for smaller landscapes or as a specimen near a patio where its cascading, patterned foliage can be appreciated up close. Provide afternoon shade in zone 8-9 to prevent leaf scorch on the variegated foliage, and plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are highly susceptible to rot in wet sites.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Merlot is a compact hybrid redbud selected for glossy, heat-tolerant purple foliage that resists the summer fading and leaf scorch common in older purple-leaf redbud cultivars like Forest Pansy.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Merlot is a hybrid redbud, a cross involving Forest Pansy and Texas redbud (Cercis canadensis var. texensis) parentage, bred to combine deep wine-purple foliage with the smaller, glossier, more heat- and drought-tolerant leaves inherited from its Texas redbud heritage. The result holds its rich purple color better through summer heat than older purple-leaf cultivars, which tend to fade to green by midsummer, and shows improved resistance to leaf scorch in hot, humid climates like the Gulf South. Rosy-pink pea-like flowers cover the bare branches in early spring before the foliage emerges, followed by the season-long purple leaf display. Its more compact, rounded habit than standard redbud makes it well suited to smaller landscapes and foundation plantings. Provide afternoon shade in the hottest climates and well-drained soil, since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites; minimal pruning is needed beyond removing crossing or damaged branches in late winter.

common_name: Ruby Falls Redbud (Weeping Purple-Leaf Dwarf Redbud)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ruby Falls combines a weeping, cascading form with deep purple foliage and a truly dwarf size, making it one of the most useful redbud cultivars for small gardens and container culture.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting where its weeping branches can cascade freely. Ruby Falls combines two desirable redbud traits rarely found together — the deep, rich purple foliage of Forest Pansy and the graceful, cascading branch structure of a weeping cultivar — on a genuinely dwarf tree that typically stays under 10 feet tall, considerably smaller than most purple-leaf redbud selections. In early spring, the weeping branches are studded with the species' typical rosy-pink, pea-like flowers before heart-shaped, glossy purple leaves emerge and hold their color well into summer. Its small mature size and weeping form make it an excellent specimen for a small garden, foundation planting, or large container, where its cascading habit and dark foliage stand out against lighter-colored companions. Provide afternoon shade in zone 8-9 to help the purple foliage resist summer fading and scorch, and plant in well-drained soil since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter.

common_name: Black Pearl Redbud (Near-Black Glossy Foliage Redbud)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Pearl is a hybrid redbud with the darkest, glossiest foliage available in the genus, holding near-black purple color through summer heat better than older purple-leaf cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Black Pearl is a hybrid redbud bred for the darkest foliage color available in the genus, with new leaves emerging nearly black-purple and holding that deep, glossy color with far less summer fading than older purple-leaf cultivars like Forest Pansy, which typically wash out to greenish-purple by midsummer. The glossy leaf surface, inherited in part from Texas redbud parentage, also reflects heat more effectively and resists leaf scorch better than standard purple-leaf redbuds in hot, humid Gulf South summers. Rosy-pink, pea-like flowers cover the bare branches in early spring before the dramatic dark foliage emerges, and the tree grows into a well-proportioned small shade tree with the redbud's typical graceful, spreading form. Provide afternoon shade in the hottest climates for the best color retention, and plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are highly susceptible to rot in wet sites. Prune only to remove dead, damaged, or crossing branches in late winter.

common_name: Branford Beauty Fern (Vigorous Silver-Painted Hybrid Lady Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Branford Beauty is a sterile hybrid between Japanese painted fern and lady fern, combining painted fern's silvery coloring with lady fern's larger size and greater vigor and heat tolerance.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Branford Beauty is a sterile hybrid between Japanese painted fern (Athyrium niponicum) and the native lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina), combining the silvery-gray frond coloring and reddish stems inherited from its painted fern parent with the larger stature, greater vigor, and improved heat tolerance of lady fern. The result is a more substantial, faster-growing plant than a typical Japanese painted fern, better able to hold up through Gulf South summer heat and humidity while retaining much of the ornamental silver coloring that makes painted ferns so popular. Fronds emerge silvery-gray with burgundy-red stems in spring, filling out into an attractive, arching clump that provides season-long texture in the shade garden. As a sterile hybrid, it does not set spores and spread by itself, making it a well-behaved choice for mixed shade plantings alongside hostas, heucheras, and other ferns. Cut back old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.
